questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: During the process of reading a sentence, the first two words are temporarily held in which type of memory system that allows you to manipulate and use information in real time?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Working Memory. Working memory is the short-term system that holds information (like the first words of a sentence) for seconds while you actively manipulate and use it. Sensory memory lasts under a second, while long-term, episodic, and semantic memory store information durably rather than supporting real-time manipulation.
questions.keyConcept: Working memory = brief store that holds and manipulates information in real time.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: During reading, the first two words are primarily processed by which of the following?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Working Memory. As you read, the opening words are held and manipulated in working memory until the sentence is understood. Short-term memory passively holds data without manipulation, and long-term/sensory/procedural systems serve durable storage, ultra-brief trace, and motor-skill roles respectively.
questions.keyConcept: Reading holds the early words in working memory for real-time processing.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A lesion involving the upper midbrain would most likely present with which of the following postural abnormalities?
options: Extension of both upper and lower limbs
Flexion of upper limbs with extension of lower limbs
Loss of coordination and intention tremor
questions.explanation: The correct answer is flexion of upper limbs with extension of lower limbs (decorticate posturing). A lesion of the upper midbrain (above the red nucleus) removes cortical drive but leaves rubrospinal facilitation of upper-limb flexors, producing arm flexion with leg extension. Extension of all four limbs (decerebrate) occurs with lower lesions below the red nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: Lesion above the red nucleus -> decorticate posture (arm flexion, leg extension).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Basic knowledge, such as facts and concepts about the world, belongs to which type of memory?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Semantic memory, which stores general facts and concepts about the world independent of personal experience. Episodic memory stores personally experienced events, procedural memory stores skills, and working memory is only transient.
questions.keyConcept: Semantic memory = general facts/concepts; episodic = personal events.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A teenager vividly remembers her 10th birthday party, including the people and events. Which of the following types of memory does this represent?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Explicit (declarative) memory. Consciously recalling a specific event such as a birthday is declarative/explicit memory (its episodic subtype). Procedural and implicit memory are unconscious skill/behavioral memories, and working memory is only transient.
questions.keyConcept: Conscious recall of events/facts = explicit (declarative) memory.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The Globus Pallidus sends major inhibitory projections to which nucleus of the Thalamus?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Ventral Anterior nucleus. The globus pallidus internus sends GABAergic inhibitory output to the ventral anterior (and ventral lateral) thalamic nuclei in the basal-ganglia motor loop. VPL/VPM are somatosensory relays, the medial geniculate is auditory, and the pulvinar is visual association.
questions.keyConcept: Globus pallidus (GPi) inhibits the VA/VL thalamic nuclei (basal-ganglia motor loop).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A young athlete sustains a head injury and later develops a severe headache followed by sudden death. Rupture of an aneurysm in which of the following structures is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Circle of Willis. Saccular (berry) aneurysms form at branch points of the Circle of Willis; rupture causes subarachnoid hemorrhage with thunderclap headache and can be rapidly fatal. Middle meningeal artery injury instead causes an epidural hematoma after temporal bone fracture.
questions.keyConcept: Berry aneurysms of the Circle of Willis rupture -> subarachnoid hemorrhage.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The Great cerebral vein (of Galen) is formed by the union of which of the following veins?
options: Right and left internal cerebral veins
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the right and left internal cerebral veins. The great cerebral vein of Galen is formed by union of the two internal cerebral veins and drains into the straight sinus. The basal veins of Rosenthal join it but do not form it.
questions.keyConcept: Great cerebral vein (of Galen) = union of the two internal cerebral veins -> straight sinus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The ansa cervicalis, a key motor component of the cervical plexus, is formed by contributions from which roots?
questions.explanation: Per the source key, the ansa cervicalis receives contributions described as both anterior and posterior roots: the superior root carries C1 fibers travelling with the hypoglossal nerve and the inferior root carries C2-C3. It is a motor loop of the cervical plexus supplying the infrahyoid (strap) muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Ansa cervicalis (C1-C3) is a motor loop of the cervical plexus supplying the strap muscles.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which artery primarily supplies the genu of the internal capsule?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Anterior Cerebral Artery. The genu and anterior limb of the internal capsule are supplied largely by the recurrent artery of Heubner, a branch of the ACA. The posterior limb is supplied mainly by lenticulostriate branches of the MCA and the anterior choroidal artery.
questions.keyConcept: Genu/anterior limb of internal capsule: recurrent artery of Heubner (from ACA).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Failure of closure of the rostral neuropore during the neurulation results in which of the following congenital anomalies?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Anencephaly. Failure of the rostral (anterior) neuropore to close (about day 25) prevents forebrain and cranial vault formation, producing anencephaly. Failure of caudal neuropore closure instead produces spina bifida.
questions.keyConcept: Rostral neuropore failure -> anencephaly; caudal neuropore failure -> spina bifida.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The Stria Medullaris of the Thalamus is a fiber bundle that primarily carries afferent fibers from which of the following structures to the Habenular Nuclei?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Septal area. The stria medullaris thalami carries afferents chiefly from the septal nuclei (with hypothalamic/limbic inputs) to the habenular nuclei of the epithalamus, which relay to the midbrain via the fasciculus retroflexus.
questions.keyConcept: Stria medullaris thalami: septal area -> habenular nuclei.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following parts are present in both the ansa cervicalis and the cervical plexus?
questions.explanation: Per the source key, the shared parts are the anterior and posterior divisions. Functionally, both the ansa cervicalis and the cervical plexus arise from the ventral rami of the upper cervical nerves (C1-C4).
questions.keyConcept: The cervical plexus and ansa cervicalis arise from ventral rami of C1-C4.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The carotid triangle and the muscular triangle are separated by which of the following muscles?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the superior belly of omohyoid. It crosses the carotid sheath and separates the carotid triangle (above) from the muscular triangle (below). Sternocleidomastoid forms the posterior boundary of the anterior triangle, not this internal division.
questions.keyConcept: Superior belly of omohyoid separates the carotid from the muscular triangle.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following white matter tracts connects different cortical areas within the same hemisphere?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Cingulum, an association fiber bundle that links cortical regions within the same hemisphere (a key limbic tract). The corpus callosum and anterior commissure are commissural (interhemispheric), and the internal capsule is a projection tract.
questions.keyConcept: Cingulum = association tract connecting cortical areas within one hemisphere.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following bones forms the medial wall of the pterygopalatine fossa?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the perpendicular plate of the palatine bone, which forms the medial wall of the pterygopalatine fossa. The sphenoid (pterygoid process) forms its posterior wall and the maxilla its anterior wall.
questions.keyConcept: Medial wall of the pterygopalatine fossa = perpendicular plate of the palatine bone.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presents with anterograde amnesia following a stroke affecting the anterior thalamic nucleus. Damage to which part of the Papez circuit is responsible for this memory deficit?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Anterior Thalamic Nucleus, the thalamic relay of the Papez circuit (mammillary body -> mammillothalamic tract -> anterior thalamic nucleus -> cingulate gyrus). Its damage interrupts memory consolidation and causes anterograde amnesia.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior thalamic nucleus is the Papez-circuit relay; lesions cause anterograde amnesia.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The mammillothalamic tract primarily sends fibers to which of the following thalamic nuclei?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Anterior thalamic nucleus. The mammillothalamic tract (of Vicq d'Azyr) projects from the mammillary bodies to the anterior thalamic nucleus, continuing the Papez circuit.
questions.keyConcept: Mammillothalamic tract: mammillary bodies -> anterior thalamic nucleus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Through which of the following do auditory radiations pass?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the sublentiform (sublenticular) part of the internal capsule, through which the auditory radiation passes to Heschl's auditory cortex. The optic radiation instead runs in the retrolentiform part.
questions.keyConcept: Auditory radiation -> sublentiform internal capsule; optic radiation -> retrolentiform.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following structures is connected by the fornix?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the hippocampus and mammillary body. The fornix is the major efferent tract of the hippocampus, projecting to the mammillary bodies (and septal area) as part of the limbic/Papez circuit.
questions.keyConcept: Fornix connects the hippocampus to the mammillary bodies.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The ventral posteromedial nucleus (VPM) of the thalamus receives afferent fibers from which of the following pathways?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the trigeminal lemniscus. The VPM nucleus relays facial/oral sensation carried by the trigeminal lemniscus, whereas body sensation (spinothalamic and dorsal column-medial lemniscus) relays in VPL.
questions.keyConcept: VPM relays facial sensation (trigeminal lemniscus); VPL relays body sensation.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the primary function of the Papez circuit?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is regulation of prolonged emotions. The Papez circuit links the hippocampus, mammillary bodies, anterior thalamus, and cingulate gyrus to mediate emotional experience and memory, not movement, vision, or balance.
questions.keyConcept: Papez circuit governs prolonged emotion and memory.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The inferior parathyroid glands and thymus are derived from which of the following pharyngeal pouches?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the third pharyngeal pouch. The inferior parathyroid glands and the thymus both develop from the third pharyngeal pouch (the thymus migrates caudally, dragging the inferior parathyroids with it). The superior parathyroids and the ultimobranchial body arise from the fourth pouch.
questions.keyConcept: Third pharyngeal pouch -> inferior parathyroids + thymus; fourth pouch -> superior parathyroids.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following structures is formed from the rhombic lip of the metencephalon?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the cerebellum. The rhombic lips of the metencephalon (derived from the alar plate) give rise to the cerebellum. The pons arises from the ventral metencephalon and the medulla from the myelencephalon.
questions.keyConcept: Rhombic lip of the metencephalon -> cerebellum.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The corticonuclear (corticobulbar) fibers primarily pass through which part of the internal capsule?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the genu of the internal capsule, which carries corticonuclear (corticobulbar) fibers to brainstem motor nuclei. Corticospinal fibers run in the posterior limb.
questions.keyConcept: Corticobulbar (corticonuclear) fibers run in the genu of the internal capsule.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following structures primarily connects the amygdala with the hypothalamus?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the stria terminalis, the main pathway connecting the amygdala to the hypothalamus (and septal area). The fornix instead links hippocampus to mammillary bodies.
questions.keyConcept: Stria terminalis connects the amygdala to the hypothalamus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following structures forms the anterior wall of the third ventricle?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the lamina terminalis, which forms the anterior wall of the third ventricle. The thalamus forms its lateral wall and the hypothalamus its floor and lower lateral wall.
questions.keyConcept: Lamina terminalis = anterior wall of the third ventricle.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: During embryological development, which of the following structures is derived from the fourth pharyngeal pouch?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the superior parathyroid glands. The fourth pharyngeal pouch gives rise to the superior parathyroid glands and the ultimobranchial body (parafollicular C cells). The inferior parathyroids and thymus arise from the third pouch.
questions.keyConcept: 4th pharyngeal pouch -> superior parathyroids + ultimobranchial body.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: In the developing hindbrain, the sensory nuclei are derived from which embryological structure?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the alar lamina (plate). In the developing neural tube the alar plate (dorsal) forms sensory nuclei, the basal plate (ventral) forms motor nuclei, and the sulcus limitans separates them.
questions.keyConcept: Alar plate -> sensory nuclei; basal plate -> motor nuclei.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following fiber tracts passes through the sublenticular part of the internal capsule?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the auditory radiation, which passes through the sublenticular part of the internal capsule to reach the auditory cortex. The optic radiation occupies the retrolenticular part.
questions.keyConcept: Auditory radiation traverses the sublenticular internal capsule.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following structures provides the primary input to the lateral geniculate body (LGB)?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the optic tract. Retinal axons travel optic nerve -> chiasma -> optic tract to synapse in the lateral geniculate body; the optic radiation then projects from the LGB to the visual cortex.
questions.keyConcept: Optic tract delivers retinal input to the lateral geniculate body.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The Ventral posteromedial nucleus (VPM) of thalamus primarily receives sensory input from which of the following pathways?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the trigeminal lemniscus. VPM is the thalamic relay for facial/oral sensation carried by the trigeminal lemniscus; the dorsal column-medial lemniscus and spinothalamic tracts relay body sensation in VPL.
questions.keyConcept: VPM relays facial sensation via the trigeminal lemniscus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following veins is located in the cisterna ambiens?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the great cerebral vein (of Galen), which lies in the cisterna ambiens (quadrigeminal cistern) and drains into the straight sinus. Although the basal vein of Rosenthal also runs nearby, the named vessel here is the great cerebral vein.
questions.keyConcept: The great cerebral vein of Galen runs in the cisterna ambiens.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following fiber tracts is a commissural fiber connecting the two cerebral hemispheres?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the forceps major, a commissural fiber of the splenium of the corpus callosum connecting the two occipital lobes. The cingulum and superior longitudinal fasciculus are association tracts, not commissural.
questions.keyConcept: Forceps major = splenial corpus callosum fibers linking the occipital lobes.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following structures lies deep to the hypoglossus muscle in the floor of the mouth?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the lingual artery, which lies deep to the hyoglossus muscle in the floor of the mouth. The lingual nerve, submandibular duct, and hypoglossal nerve all lie superficial (lateral) to hyoglossus.
questions.keyConcept: Lingual artery runs deep to hyoglossus; the nerve/duct/CN XII run superficial.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following structures forms the lateral wall of the third ventricle?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the thalamus, which forms the upper lateral wall of the third ventricle, while the hypothalamus forms the floor and lower lateral wall and the lamina terminalis the anterior wall.
questions.keyConcept: Thalamus forms the lateral wall of the third ventricle.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Fibers reaching the Lateral Geniculate Body are carried mainly by which of the following structures?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the optic tract. Fibers reaching the lateral geniculate body are carried by the optic tract; the optic radiation carries fibers onward from the LGB to the visual cortex.
questions.keyConcept: Optic tract carries retinal fibers to the lateral geniculate body.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which artery primarily supplies the genu of the internal capsule?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the Anterior Cerebral Artery, which supplies the genu and anterior limb of the internal capsule via the recurrent artery of Heubner. The MCA lenticulostriates supply the posterior limb.
questions.keyConcept: Recurrent artery of Heubner (ACA) supplies the genu of the internal capsule.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which part of the brain surrounds the third ventricle?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the diencephalon (thalamus, hypothalamus, epithalamus, subthalamus), which surrounds the third ventricle. The midbrain instead surrounds the cerebral aqueduct.
questions.keyConcept: The diencephalon surrounds the third ventricle.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following structures is connected by the fornix?
options: Links cingulate gyrus and entorhinal cortex
Uncinate fasciculus – links frontal and temporal lobes
Fornix – connects hippocampus to mammillary bodies
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the fornix, which connects the hippocampus to the mammillary bodies. The corpus callosum and anterior commissure are interhemispheric commissures, and the uncinate fasciculus links frontal and temporal lobes.
questions.keyConcept: Fornix: hippocampus -> mammillary bodies.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which structure connects the amygdala to the hypothalamus?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the stria terminalis, the principal tract connecting the amygdala to the hypothalamus. The fornix instead connects hippocampus to mammillary bodies.
questions.keyConcept: Stria terminalis connects amygdala to hypothalamus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following fibers pass through the genu of the internal capsule?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is corticonuclear (corticobulbar) fibers, which pass through the genu of the internal capsule to brainstem motor nuclei; corticospinal fibers occupy the posterior limb.
questions.keyConcept: Genu of internal capsule carries corticonuclear (corticobulbar) fibers.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient with severe brain injury is observed to have flexion of the upper limbs and extension of the lower limbs in response to painful stimuli. This posture is most consistent with a lesion involving the:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the upper midbrain. Decorticate posturing (upper-limb flexion, lower-limb extension) localizes to a lesion above the red nucleus in the upper midbrain; extension of all limbs (decerebrate) indicates a lower lesion.
questions.keyConcept: Decorticate posture (arm flexion/leg extension) -> lesion above the red nucleus (upper midbrain).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following investigations records the spontaneous electrical activity of the brain?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is electroencephalography (EEG), which records the spontaneous electrical activity of the cerebral cortex. ECG records the heart, EMG records muscle, and MRI/CT are structural imaging.
questions.keyConcept: EEG records spontaneous cortical electrical activity.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The Reticular Activating System plays an important role in maintaining wakefulness and consciousness. Which of the following properties best characterizes this system?
options: Dependence solely on cortical input for activation
Activity limited only during deep sleep
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that it has intrinsic activity. The reticular activating system generates spontaneous neuronal discharge that maintains cortical arousal and wakefulness, rather than depending solely on sensory or cortical input.
questions.keyConcept: The reticular activating system has intrinsic (spontaneous) activity maintaining arousal.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following best describes an electroencephalogram (EEG)?
options: Record of spontaneous electrical activity of the brain during conscious state
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that an EEG is a record of the spontaneous electrical activity of the brain (cortex), typically in the conscious/resting state. It does not record muscle activity, CSF pressure, or blood flow.
questions.keyConcept: EEG = recording of the brain's spontaneous cortical electrical activity.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following best describes the characteristic of the reticular excitatory area?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is that it has intrinsic activity. The reticular excitatory (activating) area discharges spontaneously to drive cortical arousal, independent of external input.
questions.keyConcept: The reticular excitatory area has intrinsic spontaneous activity.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Decerebrate rigidity is caused by which of the following mechanisms?
options: Lesion of the cerebral cortex leading to upper limb flexion
Lesion of the cerebellum causing ataxia
Lesion of the basal ganglia causing tremor
Lesion of the spinal cord causing flaccid paralysis
questions.explanation: The correct answer is unopposed pontine reticular formation. A midbrain transection removes inhibitory cortical/medullary input, leaving the pontine reticular formation and vestibular nuclei to drive extensor tone unopposed -> decerebrate rigidity.
questions.keyConcept: Decerebrate rigidity = unopposed pontine reticular formation/vestibular extensor drive.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which type of brain wave is primarily produced during deep (slow-wave) sleep?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is delta waves, the high-amplitude, low-frequency (<4 Hz) waves of deep slow-wave (NREM stage 3) sleep. Alpha occurs in relaxed wakefulness, beta in alertness, and theta in light sleep.
questions.keyConcept: Delta waves (<4 Hz) dominate deep slow-wave (NREM) sleep.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following is a characteristic of slow-wave sleep (NREM sleep)?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is a low threshold of arousal: slow-wave (NREM) sleep is easily interrupted. Rapid eye movements, vivid dreaming, muscle atonia, and irregular vitals are features of REM sleep.
questions.keyConcept: NREM (slow-wave) sleep has a low arousal threshold; REM has atonia and vivid dreams.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following happens in NREM?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is sleep talking and walking (somnambulism), which occur during deep NREM sleep. Muscle atonia, vivid dreams, and irregular heart rate/respiration characterize REM sleep.
questions.keyConcept: Sleepwalking and sleep-talking occur in NREM sleep.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following phenomena is characteristic of NREM Sleep?
options: Rapid eye movements and vivid dreaming
Increased brain metabolic activity similar to wakefulness
questions.explanation: The correct answer is sleep-walking and sleep-talking, parasomnias of NREM sleep. REM sleep is characterized by rapid eye movements, atonia, vivid dreams, and autonomic variability.
questions.keyConcept: Somnambulism and sleep-talking are NREM parasomnias.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following hormones shows a decrease in secretion during REM sleep?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is growth hormone. GH secretion peaks during deep NREM (slow-wave) sleep and falls during REM, whereas cortisol rises later in the sleep cycle.
questions.keyConcept: Growth hormone surges in NREM (slow-wave) sleep and falls during REM.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The categorical hemisphere is primarily responsible for which of the following functions?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is language. The categorical (dominant, usually left) hemisphere handles language and analytic, sequential processing; the representational hemisphere handles music, spatial, and facial perception.
questions.keyConcept: Categorical (dominant) hemisphere = language and analytic processing.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which hemisphere of the brain is primarily responsible for solving mathematical problems and analytical reasoning?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the categorical hemisphere, which handles mathematics, language, and analytical reasoning (dominant, usually left). The representational (right) hemisphere handles spatial/holistic tasks.
questions.keyConcept: Categorical hemisphere handles math, language, and analytic reasoning.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following functions is primarily associated with the left cerebral hemisphere?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is information processing: the categorical (left) hemisphere performs detailed, sequential/analytic information processing and language. Spatial awareness, face recognition, and music belong to the right (representational) hemisphere.
questions.keyConcept: Left (categorical) hemisphere = analytic, detailed information processing.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Recognition of faces is primarily a function of which of the following?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the representational (non-dominant, usually right) hemisphere, which specializes in facial recognition and spatial/holistic processing. The categorical hemisphere handles language and analysis.
questions.keyConcept: Face recognition is a representational (right) hemisphere function.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following best describes the primary function of the left cerebral hemisphere?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is detailed processing: the left (categorical) hemisphere handles fine, analytic, sequential processing and language, whereas spatial, emotional, and musical functions are right-hemisphere.
questions.keyConcept: Left hemisphere = detailed, analytic processing.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following functions is primarily associated with the categorical (usually left) cerebral hemisphere?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is mathematical operations. The categorical (usually left) hemisphere governs mathematics, language, and logical analysis; artistic, spatial, and facial functions are representational (right).
questions.keyConcept: Categorical (left) hemisphere performs mathematical and logical operations.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A right-handed patient suffers a stroke and subsequently develops impaired analytical thinking, difficulty with detailed processing, and language dysfunction. Which cerebral hemisphere is most likely affected?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the left hemisphere. In a right-handed person the left hemisphere is dominant for language and analytic/detailed processing, so its damage causes aphasia and impaired analytic thinking.
questions.keyConcept: In right-handers, the left (dominant) hemisphere controls language and analytic processing.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following brain regions is primarily responsible for word production?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Broca's area in the inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere, responsible for motor speech production and word articulation. Wernicke's area handles comprehension, while the angular and supramarginal gyri integrate reading and written language.
questions.keyConcept: Broca's area (inferior frontal gyrus) = motor speech/word production.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: primarily involved in language comprehension and the processing of thoughts into meaningful speech?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Wernicke's area in the posterior superior temporal gyrus, responsible for language comprehension and turning thoughts into meaningful speech. Broca's area instead governs speech production.
questions.keyConcept: Wernicke's area = language comprehension.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following statements about the neural control of speech is FALSE?
options: Broca's area – responsible for speech production
Wernicke's area is responsible for language comprehension
Primary motor cortex controls articulatory muscles
Sensory areas is responsible vocalization and writing
Arcuate fasciculus connects Broca's and Wernicke's areas
questions.explanation: The FALSE statement is that sensory areas are responsible for vocalization and writing, which are motor functions of Broca's area and the motor cortex. The other statements correctly describe Broca's, Wernicke's, the motor cortex, and the arcuate fasciculus.
questions.keyConcept: Vocalization and writing are motor (Broca's/motor cortex), not sensory, functions.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Lesions of the parieto-occipitotemporal region are most likely to produce which of the following clinical findings?
options: Non-fluent, effortful speech with relatively preserved comprehension
Fluent but meaningless speech with impaired comprehension
Contralateral spastic paralysis with preserved language
Ataxia with impaired coordination and balance
questions.explanation: The correct answer is fluent but meaningless speech with impaired comprehension. A parieto-occipitotemporal (Wernicke) lesion produces receptive (Wernicke) aphasia; non-fluent effortful speech with preserved comprehension is Broca (expressive) aphasia.
questions.keyConcept: Wernicke (receptive) aphasia = fluent, meaningless speech with poor comprehension.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following brain regions is primarily responsible for word production?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Broca's area, which controls motor speech and word production in the dominant inferior frontal gyrus. Wernicke's area and the angular gyrus serve comprehension and reading, not word production.
questions.keyConcept: Broca's area produces speech (word articulation).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A patient presents with flaccid dysarthria. Which of the following is the most characteristic feature?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is weak, nasal speech. Flaccid dysarthria reflects lower motor neuron/bulbar weakness with palatal incompetence, producing breathy, hypernasal speech. Scanning speech is cerebellar (ataxic) and strained-strangled voice is spastic dysarthria.
questions.keyConcept: Flaccid dysarthria (LMN/bulbar) -> weak, breathy, nasal speech.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following sequences correctly represents the pathway for seeing an object and then speaking about it?
options: Visual cortex → Broca's area → Wernicke's area → Primary motor cortex
Visual cortex → Wernicke's area → Broca's area → Primary motor cortex
Wernicke's area → Visual cortex → Broca's area → Primary motor cortex
Visual cortex → Primary motor cortex → Wernicke's area → Broca's area
Broca's area → Visual cortex → Wernicke's area → Primary motor cortex
questions.explanation: The correct sequence is visual cortex -> Wernicke's area -> Broca's area -> primary motor cortex. The seen word is recognized/comprehended in Wernicke's area, transmitted via the arcuate fasciculus to Broca's area for speech planning, then executed by the motor cortex.
questions.keyConcept: Seeing then speaking: visual cortex -> Wernicke -> Broca -> motor cortex.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following brain regions is primarily involved in the formulation of thoughts and language comprehension?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Wernicke's area, central to language comprehension and the formulation of thoughts into language. Broca's area handles speech output rather than comprehension.
questions.keyConcept: Wernicke's area = comprehension and language formulation.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A patient is unable to repeat words despite relatively preserved comprehension and fluent speech. This language disorder is most consistent with:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is conduction aphasia. Impaired repetition with preserved fluency and comprehension results from damage to the arcuate fasciculus, which disconnects Wernicke's from Broca's areas.
questions.keyConcept: Conduction aphasia = impaired repetition from an arcuate fasciculus lesion.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following functions is performed by the neocortex?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is odor discrimination. The neocortex performs higher discriminative functions such as distinguishing odors, whereas basic smell perception is a primitive (paleocortex/olfactory) function and hormonal/autonomic/reflex control are subcortical.
questions.keyConcept: Neocortex performs fine odor discrimination (basic smell = paleocortex).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Stimulation of the Amygdala is most commonly associated with which of the following emotional responses?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is fear. The amygdala is the limbic hub for processing fear and threat, so its stimulation characteristically evokes fear and defensive/rage responses.
questions.keyConcept: Amygdala stimulation evokes fear.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A patient develops persistent fever after a head injury. Which of the following sites is most likely affected?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the anterior hypothalamus, the heat-loss (heat-dissipation) center. Its damage impairs heat loss and causes persistent central hyperthermia/fever, whereas the posterior hypothalamus governs heat conservation.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior hypothalamus = heat-loss center; damage -> central hyperthermia.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following is the primary function of the limbic lobe?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is consolidation of memory. The limbic lobe's primary roles are emotion and memory consolidation, not voluntary movement, visual reflexes, balance, or respiration.
questions.keyConcept: The limbic lobe is key for memory consolidation.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A boy falls off his bike and later develops mild fever without signs of infection or inflammation. Which part of the limbic system is most likely involved in regulating this autonomic response?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the anterior hypothalamus, which regulates heat loss and autonomic thermoregulation; its involvement can cause a non-infectious (central) fever. The posterior hypothalamus instead conserves heat.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior hypothalamus controls heat loss and autonomic thermoregulation.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following functions is not primarily associated with the limbic system?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is temperature regulation, which is a hypothalamic homeostatic function rather than a primary limbic role. The limbic system handles emotion, memory, motivation, and reward.
questions.keyConcept: Temperature regulation is hypothalamic, not a primary limbic function.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following functions is primarily associated with the periventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is aversion. The periventricular hypothalamic region mediates aversion/punishment responses, whereas hunger/thirst, thermoregulation, circadian rhythm, and reproductive hormone release map to other hypothalamic nuclei.
questions.keyConcept: The periventricular hypothalamic nucleus mediates aversion.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following fiber tracts is an important component of the Papez circuit, connecting the cingulate gyrus to the hippocampal formation?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the cingulum, the Papez-circuit association tract linking the cingulate gyrus to the hippocampal formation. The fornix instead links the hippocampus to the mammillary bodies.
questions.keyConcept: Cingulum links the cingulate gyrus to the hippocampal formation (Papez circuit).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following functions is primarily associated with the amygdaloid nucleus?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is feeling pleasure. The amygdaloid nucleus processes emotional responses including pleasure and reward (as well as fear/rage); it is not involved in movement, thermoregulation, language, or vision.
questions.keyConcept: The amygdala processes emotion, including pleasure and fear.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following terms describes the process by which the nervous system ignores or reduces responses to repetitive, non-threatening stimuli? (ignore the unwanted)
questions.explanation: The correct answer is habituation, the progressive reduction of response to a repeated non-threatening stimulus (a basic form of non-associative learning). Sensitization is the opposite, and classical conditioning is associative learning.
questions.keyConcept: Habituation = reduced response to repeated harmless stimuli (non-associative learning).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which neurotransmitter is primarily involved in the brain's pleasure and reward pathways?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is dopamine, the principal neurotransmitter of the mesolimbic reward/pleasure pathway. Serotonin, norepinephrine, acetylcholine, and GABA serve other roles.
questions.keyConcept: Dopamine drives the brain's reward/pleasure pathway.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which part of the brain is primarily responsible for temperature homeostasis?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the hypothalamus, the master center for temperature homeostasis that integrates thermal input and drives heat loss or conservation. The medulla controls cardiorespiratory reflexes, not core temperature.
questions.keyConcept: The hypothalamus is the body's thermostat for temperature homeostasis.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following functions is primarily involved in the limbic system?
questions.explanation: Among the listed options the source marks procedural learning; the limbic system's core roles are emotion and memory/learning. Note that purely motor procedural learning also heavily involves the basal ganglia and cerebellum, whereas temperature regulation, executive function, and visual processing are clearly non-limbic.
questions.keyConcept: The limbic system's core roles are emotion and memory/learning.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which part of the brain surrounds the third ventricle?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the diencephalon (thalamus, hypothalamus, epithalamus, subthalamus), which surrounds the third ventricle. The midbrain instead surrounds the cerebral aqueduct.
questions.keyConcept: The diencephalon surrounds the third ventricle.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A patient presents with anterograde amnesia following a stroke affecting the anterior thalamic nucleus. Damage to which part of the Papez circuit is responsible for this memory deficit?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the anterior thalamic nucleus, the thalamic relay of the Papez circuit. Its damage interrupts memory consolidation and produces anterograde amnesia.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior thalamic nucleus relays the Papez circuit; lesions cause anterograde amnesia.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The mammillothalamic tract primarily sends fibers to which of the following thalamic nuclei?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the anterior thalamic nucleus. The mammillothalamic tract projects from the mammillary bodies to the anterior thalamic nucleus, continuing the Papez circuit.
questions.keyConcept: Mammillothalamic tract: mammillary bodies -> anterior thalamic nucleus.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following structures is connected by the fornix?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is the hippocampus and mammillary body. The fornix is the major hippocampal efferent tract projecting to the mammillary bodies in the limbic/Papez circuit.
questions.keyConcept: Fornix connects the hippocampus to the mammillary bodies.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What is the primary function of the Papez circuit?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is regulation of prolonged emotions. The Papez circuit links the hippocampus, mammillary bodies, anterior thalamus, and cingulate gyrus to mediate emotion and memory.
questions.keyConcept: The Papez circuit governs prolonged emotion and memory.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following is the primary function of the limbic lobe?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is consolidation of memory, the primary role of the limbic lobe (along with emotion). It is not involved in balance, voluntary movement, vision, or respiration.
questions.keyConcept: The limbic lobe consolidates memory.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which type of memory is responsible for storing general knowledge, facts, and basic concepts (e.g., meanings of words and world knowledge)?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is semantic memory, which stores general knowledge, facts, and concepts (e.g., word meanings). Episodic memory stores personal events and procedural memory stores skills.
questions.keyConcept: Semantic memory = general facts and concepts.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which type of memory is responsible for storing general knowledge, facts, and basic concepts (e.g., meanings of words and world knowledge)?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is semantic memory, the store of general world knowledge and concepts. Episodic, procedural, and working memory serve personal events, skills, and transient processing respectively.
questions.keyConcept: Semantic memory = general facts and concepts.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 28-year-old pregnant woman at 39 weeks' gestation is found to be colonized with Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B Streptococcus). She is admitted in active labor. To prevent neonatal infection, which of the following interventions is most appropriate?
options: Administer ampicillin antepartum at 36 weeks during routine prenatal screening
Administer ampicillin intrapartum at the time of delivery
Give the newborn a dose of ampicillin immediately after birth
Delay antibiotic prophylaxis until after delivery to avoid maternal hypotension
Administer a single oral dose of penicillin to the mother at 38 weeks
questions.explanation: The correct answer is intrapartum ampicillin. GBS-colonized mothers receive penicillin or ampicillin during labor to prevent early-onset neonatal GBS sepsis/meningitis. Antepartum treatment does not prevent recolonization, and treating only the newborn is less effective.
questions.keyConcept: GBS-colonized mothers get intrapartum ampicillin/penicillin to prevent neonatal GBS disease.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 67-year-old patient presents with acute bacterial meningitis. Empiric therapy is started before culture results are available. Which of the following regimens is the recommended first-line empiric treatment for adults in this age group?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is vancomycin + ampicillin + ceftriaxone. In older adults, ceftriaxone covers pneumococcus/meningococcus, vancomycin covers resistant pneumococcus, and ampicillin adds essential Listeria coverage.
questions.keyConcept: Empiric meningitis in older adults: vancomycin + ceftriaxone + ampicillin (ampicillin for Listeria).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs is primarily used for the treatment of cognitive symptoms in Alzheimer's disease?
questions.explanation: The correct (keyed) answer is rivastigmine, a cholinesterase inhibitor used to treat cognitive symptoms in Alzheimer's disease. Note donepezil and galantamine are also cholinesterase inhibitors, while memantine is an NMDA antagonist and selegiline an MAO-B inhibitor.
questions.keyConcept: Rivastigmine is a cholinesterase inhibitor for Alzheimer's cognitive symptoms.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is considered a second-line screening tool at the community level for early detection of cardiovascular risk?
options: Fasting blood glucose – first-line for diabetes
questions.explanation: The correct (keyed) answer is lipid profile as a second-line community screening tool for cardiovascular risk. Blood pressure, BMI, and fasting glucose are first-line screening measures, and ECG is diagnostic rather than a screening test.
questions.keyConcept: Lipid profile = second-line community CV-risk screening; BP/BMI/glucose are first-line.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is the specific antitoxin used in tetanus management?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is tetanus immune globulin (TIG), the specific antitoxin that neutralizes unbound tetanospasmin. Metronidazole/penicillin kill the organism, toxoid provides active immunization, and diazepam controls spasms.
questions.keyConcept: Tetanus immune globulin (TIG) is the specific antitoxin neutralizing tetanospasmin.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is considered the first-line disease-modifying therapy for multiple sclerosis (MS)?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is interferon beta-1, a first-line disease-modifying therapy for relapsing-remitting MS (along with glatiramer acetate). Natalizumab, fingolimod, and mitoxantrone are second-line or reserved for aggressive disease.
questions.keyConcept: Interferon beta-1 is a first-line disease-modifying therapy for MS.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: For children under 5 years of age exposed to rabies, the minimum post-exposure prophylaxis regimen consists of how many doses of rabies vaccine?
questions.explanation: The correct (keyed) answer is 2 doses for the regimen described. Clinically, complete rabies post-exposure prophylaxis combines prompt wound care, rabies immunoglobulin, and a multi-dose vaccine series.
questions.keyConcept: Rabies post-exposure prophylaxis relies on prompt vaccination plus immunoglobulin.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs is used in the treatment of chronic alcoholism and causes nausea and vomiting when alcohol is consumed?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is disulfiram, which inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase; drinking alcohol then causes acetaldehyde build-up with flushing, nausea, and vomiting, deterring use. Naltrexone and acamprosate reduce craving by other mechanisms.
questions.keyConcept: Disulfiram blocks aldehyde dehydrogenase -> aversive reaction to alcohol.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following antipsychotic drugs is preferred for treating psychosis in patients with Parkinson's disease because it has minimal extrapyramidal side effects?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is quetiapine, preferred (with clozapine) for psychosis in Parkinson's disease because its weak D2 antagonism causes minimal extrapyramidal worsening. Haloperidol and risperidone strongly block D2 and worsen parkinsonism.
questions.keyConcept: Quetiapine treats Parkinson's psychosis with minimal extrapyramidal effects.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs is administered immediately with antibiotics to reduce inflammation and neurological complications in bacterial meningitis?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is dexamethasone, given with or just before the first antibiotic dose in bacterial (especially pneumococcal) meningitis to reduce the inflammatory response and neurological complications such as hearing loss.
questions.keyConcept: Adjunctive dexamethasone in bacterial meningitis reduces inflammatory complications.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following antibiotics is commonly administered intrathecally to treat central nervous system infections?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is an aminoglycoside. Aminoglycosides penetrate the CSF poorly, so they may be administered intrathecally to treat certain CNS infections directly.
questions.keyConcept: Aminoglycosides penetrate CSF poorly and may be given intrathecally.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs is primarily used to slow disease progression in patients with Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is riluzole, which slows ALS progression by reducing glutamate excitotoxicity (inhibiting glutamate release and blocking sodium channels). The other drugs treat unrelated conditions.
questions.keyConcept: Riluzole slows ALS progression by reducing glutamate excitotoxicity.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is the most common adverse effect of Rivastigmine?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is diarrhea. Rivastigmine is a cholinesterase inhibitor, so by raising acetylcholine it causes cholinergic GI effects (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea) most commonly.
questions.keyConcept: Cholinesterase inhibitors (rivastigmine) cause cholinergic GI effects like diarrhea.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is considered a social risk factor in the elderly?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is abuse, neglect, and violence, which are social risk factors in the elderly. Hypertension, smoking, osteoporosis, and sensory impairment are medical/physical risk factors.
questions.keyConcept: Abuse, neglect, and violence are social risk factors in the elderly.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is the recommended chemoprophylaxis for close contacts of a patient with Neisseria meningitidis infection?
questions.explanation: The correct (keyed) answer is rifampin for 2 days for close contacts of Neisseria meningitidis; single-dose ciprofloxacin or ceftriaxone are also accepted chemoprophylaxis options.
questions.keyConcept: Meningococcal contacts: rifampin x2 days (or single-dose cipro/ceftriaxone).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What is the primary mechanism of action of memantine?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is NMDA receptor antagonism. Memantine blocks NMDA receptors to limit glutamate excitotoxicity in moderate-to-severe Alzheimer's disease, unlike the cholinesterase inhibitors.
questions.keyConcept: Memantine works by NMDA receptor antagonism.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What is the main mechanism of action of riluzole in the treatment of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is sodium channel blockade. Riluzole blocks sodium channels and inhibits glutamate release, reducing excitotoxicity in ALS.
questions.keyConcept: Riluzole blocks Na+ channels and glutamate release in ALS.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: In the management of a patient with penicillin-resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae, which of the following antibiotics is most appropriate to add?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is vancomycin, added (often with ceftriaxone) for penicillin-resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae. The other listed agents lack reliable activity against resistant pneumococcus in meningitis.
questions.keyConcept: Add vancomycin for penicillin-resistant pneumococcus.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 67-year-old woman presents with fever, neck stiffness, and altered mental status. Suspected bacterial meningitis is considered. Which of the following is the most appropriate empirical treatment?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is vancomycin + ceftriaxone + ampicillin. In an older adult with suspected bacterial meningitis, this empiric regimen covers resistant pneumococcus, meningococcus, and Listeria.
questions.keyConcept: Empiric meningitis in older adults: vancomycin + ceftriaxone + ampicillin.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs facilitates GABAergic neurotransmission, has no significant anxiolytic effect, and whose action can be reversed by flumazenil?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is zolpidem, a non-benzodiazepine Z-drug that selectively activates BZ1 (alpha-1) GABA-A receptors to cause sedation with little anxiolytic or muscle-relaxant effect, and is reversed by flumazenil.
questions.keyConcept: Zolpidem is a BZ1-selective Z-drug hypnotic; reversed by flumazenil.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following non-benzodiazepine hypnotics is used for insomnia, acts selectively on BZ1 receptors, and lacks significant muscle relaxant effects?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is eszopiclone, a non-benzodiazepine hypnotic acting selectively at BZ1 receptors for insomnia, lacking significant muscle-relaxant effect.
questions.keyConcept: Eszopiclone = non-benzodiazepine BZ1-selective hypnotic for insomnia.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is the specific antidote for midazolam toxicity?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is flumazenil, the specific GABA-A benzodiazepine-site antagonist that reverses benzodiazepine (midazolam) toxicity. Naloxone reverses opioids and N-acetylcysteine treats paracetamol overdose.
questions.keyConcept: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepine toxicity.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs is used for migraine prophylaxis and can also help improve insomnia?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is amitriptyline, a tricyclic antidepressant used for migraine prophylaxis that, being sedating, also improves comorbid insomnia. Sumatriptan and ergotamine are acute migraine treatments.
questions.keyConcept: Amitriptyline (TCA) prevents migraine and aids sleep due to sedation.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs is commonly used for the management of panic attacks?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is alprazolam, a short-acting benzodiazepine used for acute panic attacks. SSRIs are for long-term control, while buspirone and propranolol address other anxiety components.
questions.keyConcept: Alprazolam (benzodiazepine) treats acute panic attacks.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs acts as a GABA agonist with anticonvulsant properties?
questions.explanation: The correct (keyed) answer is zolpidem, identified as the GABA-A (BZ1)-enhancing agent among the options. The others (phenytoin, carbamazepine, valproate, ethosuximide) are classic antiepileptics acting mainly on ion channels.
questions.keyConcept: Zolpidem enhances GABA-A (BZ1) transmission.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following sedative–hypnotic drugs used for insomnia can have its effects reversed by flumazenil?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is zolpidem; as a benzodiazepine-site GABA-A agonist its sedative effect is reversible by flumazenil. Barbiturates, antihistamines, melatonin, and chloral hydrate act by other mechanisms.
questions.keyConcept: Zolpidem's effect is reversed by flumazenil (GABA-A BZ site).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient undergoing an endoscopic procedure becomes excessively sedated after receiving midazolam. He develops respiratory depression and decreased responsiveness. Which of the following is the most appropriate antidote?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is flumazenil, the antidote for benzodiazepine (midazolam) over-sedation and respiratory depression. Naloxone is for opioids; physostigmine and N-acetylcysteine treat other toxidromes.
questions.keyConcept: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepine (midazolam) over-sedation.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following local anesthetic agents uniquely provides both local anesthesia and a vasoconstrictive effect?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is cocaine, the only local anesthetic that also produces vasoconstriction (by blocking norepinephrine reuptake), so it needs no added epinephrine. Other -caine agents cause vasodilation.
questions.keyConcept: Cocaine is the only local anesthetic that is also a vasoconstrictor.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following anesthetic agents is contraindicated in a patient with ischemic heart disease (IHD)?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is isoflurane, which can cause coronary steal by dilating normal coronary vessels and diverting flow from stenosed ones, so it is avoided in ischemic heart disease.
questions.keyConcept: Isoflurane risks coronary steal-avoid in ischemic heart disease.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following anesthetic agents is preferred in a patient with hypotension
questions.explanation: The correct answer is ketamine, preferred in hypotension because its sympathomimetic action maintains blood pressure and cardiac output (and it bronchodilates). Propofol and thiopental cause hypotension.
questions.keyConcept: Ketamine supports blood pressure (sympathomimetic)-good in hypotension.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following intravenous anesthetic agents is particularly useful in patients with Bronchial Asthma and Hypotension?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is ketamine, favored in asthmatic, hypotensive patients because it is a bronchodilator and its sympathomimetic action maintains blood pressure. Propofol and thiopental can cause hypotension and bronchospasm risk.
questions.keyConcept: Ketamine = bronchodilator + BP support; ideal in asthma with hypotension.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 35-year-old patient with bronchial asthma requires general anesthesia. Which of the following anesthetic agents is preferred due to its bronchodilatory effects and hemodynamic stability?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is ketamine, preferred for asthmatics needing anesthesia because of its bronchodilatory effect and hemodynamic stability. Thiopental and propofol are less suitable here.
questions.keyConcept: Ketamine is the anesthetic of choice in bronchial asthma.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient with hypotension is scheduled to undergo surgery. Which of the following anesthetic agents is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is ketamine, the most appropriate induction agent in hypotension because its sympathomimetic activity supports blood pressure and cardiac output. Propofol and thiopental lower blood pressure.
questions.keyConcept: Ketamine maintains blood pressure in hypotensive patients.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following anesthetic agents is preferred in patients with bronchial asthma and hypotension due to its bronchodilatory and cardiovascular properties?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is ketamine, preferred in bronchial asthma with hypotension for its bronchodilatory and cardiovascular-supporting (sympathomimetic) properties.
questions.keyConcept: Ketamine: bronchodilation plus cardiovascular support.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following anesthetic agents can be used to treat cardiac arrhythmias due to its antiarrhythmic properties?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is lidocaine, which is both a local anesthetic and a class Ib antiarrhythmic (blocks cardiac sodium channels) used for ventricular arrhythmias.
questions.keyConcept: Lidocaine doubles as a class Ib antiarrhythmic for ventricular arrhythmias.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient with ischemic heart disease is scheduled for surgery under general anesthesia. Which of the following inhalational anesthetic agents is relatively contraindicated because it may precipitate coronary steal phenomenon?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is isoflurane, relatively contraindicated in ischemic heart disease because it can precipitate coronary steal by dilating healthy coronaries and diverting flow from stenosed vessels.
questions.keyConcept: Isoflurane can precipitate coronary steal in ischemic heart disease.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following antiepileptic drugs is most commonly associated with Stevens-Johnson syndrome?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is lamotrigine, the antiepileptic most associated with Stevens-Johnson syndrome, especially with rapid titration or co-administration with valproate. Slow titration reduces the risk.
questions.keyConcept: Lamotrigine is most linked to Stevens-Johnson syndrome (titrate slowly).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following antiepileptic drugs is considered the drug of choice for Trigeminal Neuralgia?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is carbamazepine, the drug of choice for trigeminal neuralgia; it reduces neuronal firing via sodium-channel blockade.
questions.keyConcept: Carbamazepine is first-line for trigeminal neuralgia.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs is commonly used for the prophylaxis of Migraine?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is propranolol, a beta-blocker that is first-line for migraine prophylaxis. Sumatriptan and ergotamine are acute (abortive) treatments.
questions.keyConcept: Propranolol (beta-blocker) is first-line migraine prophylaxis.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs is commonly used for chronic migraine prophylaxis?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is propranolol for chronic migraine prophylaxis. Sumatriptan is abortive, and topiramate/amitriptyline are alternative preventives.
questions.keyConcept: Propranolol is a first-line migraine preventive.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs is considered the safest for treating absence seizures in children, with minimal impact on cognition and learning?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is ethosuximide, the safest first-line drug for childhood absence seizures (blocks T-type calcium channels) with minimal cognitive impact. Valproate is an effective alternative.
questions.keyConcept: Ethosuximide is first-line for childhood absence seizures (T-type Ca2+ blocker).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs is first-line for the acute treatment of moderate to severe migraine attacks?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is sumatriptan, a 5-HT1B/1D agonist that is first-line for acute moderate-to-severe migraine via cranial vasoconstriction and inhibition of CGRP release.
questions.keyConcept: Sumatriptan (triptan) is first-line for acute moderate-severe migraine.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following Benzodiazepines is commonly used for the management of Status Epilepticus due to its rapid onset of action and reliable anticonvulsant effect?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is lorazepam, the IV benzodiazepine of choice to abort status epilepticus due to rapid onset and long CNS duration. Phenytoin is used for subsequent control.
questions.keyConcept: IV lorazepam is first-line to stop status epilepticus.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs is most commonly associated with gingival hyperplasia as a side effect?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is phenytoin, which classically causes gingival hyperplasia, along with hirsutism and ataxia.
questions.keyConcept: Phenytoin causes gingival hyperplasia.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs is commonly used for prophylaxis of migraine?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is propranolol, a first-line beta-blocker for migraine prophylaxis. Amitriptyline and topiramate are alternative preventives; sumatriptan is abortive.
questions.keyConcept: Propranolol is first-line migraine prophylaxis.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs is associated with gingival hyperplasia and may be less suitable for certain patients, including females?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is phenytoin, associated with gingival hyperplasia and cosmetically troublesome effects such as hirsutism and coarsening of features.
questions.keyConcept: Phenytoin causes gingival hyperplasia (and hirsutism).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs is commonly associated with dilutional hyponatremia as an adverse effect?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is carbamazepine, which commonly causes dilutional hyponatremia through an SIADH-like effect (water retention).
questions.keyConcept: Carbamazepine causes dilutional hyponatremia (SIADH-like).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient on long-term treatment for trigeminal neuralgia develops hyponatremia with low serum osmolality and symptoms of water intoxication. Which of the following drugs is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is carbamazepine. Long-term use (e.g., for trigeminal neuralgia) can cause hyponatremia with low serum osmolality and water intoxication via an SIADH-like mechanism.
questions.keyConcept: Carbamazepine causes SIADH-like hyponatremia with water intoxication.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What is the primary mechanism of action of sumatriptan?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is 5-HT1B/1D receptor agonism. Sumatriptan agonizes 5-HT1B/1D receptors, causing cranial vasoconstriction and inhibiting neuropeptide (CGRP) release to abort migraine.
questions.keyConcept: Sumatriptan = 5-HT1B/1D receptor agonist.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman reports frequent, recurrent headache attacks occurring more than 10 days per month, associated with nausea and photophobia. Her physician decides to start a medication to reduce the frequency of future attacks rather than treat acute pain episodes. Which of the following drugs is most appropriate for prophylaxis of Chronic migraine?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is propranolol for prophylaxis of chronic migraine (frequent attacks). Sumatriptan, ergotamine, and metoclopramide treat acute attacks rather than prevent them.
questions.keyConcept: Propranolol prevents chronic/frequent migraine.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following antidepressant drugs is associated with a low incidence of sexual dysfunction?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is bupropion, a norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor with a low incidence of sexual dysfunction, unlike SSRIs (fluoxetine, paroxetine, sertraline) and TCAs.
questions.keyConcept: Bupropion (NDRI) causes minimal sexual dysfunction.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which antidepressant is associated with minimal sexual dysfunction compared to SSRIs?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is mirtazapine, a noradrenergic and specific serotonergic antidepressant that causes little sexual dysfunction compared with SSRIs.
questions.keyConcept: Mirtazapine causes minimal sexual dysfunction.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following antidepressants is least likely to cause sexual dysfunction?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is mirtazapine, least likely among the options to cause sexual dysfunction because it does not increase synaptic serotonin the way SSRIs/SNRIs do.
questions.keyConcept: Mirtazapine is least likely to cause sexual dysfunction.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following antidepressants is least likely to cause sexual dysfunction in patients?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is mirtazapine, which causes minimal sexual dysfunction; SSRIs (fluoxetine, sertraline, paroxetine) and the SNRI venlafaxine commonly do.
questions.keyConcept: Mirtazapine spares sexual function compared with SSRIs/SNRIs.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs is used both as an antidepressant and for smoking cessation?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is bupropion, used both as an antidepressant and as an aid to smoking cessation (it reduces craving and withdrawal).
questions.keyConcept: Bupropion treats depression and aids smoking cessation.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs is an antidepressant that is not an SSRI?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is mirtazapine, which is not an SSRI; it is a noradrenergic and specific serotonergic antidepressant (NaSSA). The others listed are SSRIs.
questions.keyConcept: Mirtazapine is a NaSSA, not an SSRI.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman with relapsing–remitting multiple sclerosis continues to have relapses despite first-line disease-modifying therapy. Her neurologist decides to escalate treatment and starts a monthly intravenous therapy. Which of the following is the most likely drug?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is natalizumab, a monthly IV monoclonal antibody (anti-alpha4-integrin) used as escalation therapy for relapsing-remitting MS that fails first-line agents (carries a risk of PML).
questions.keyConcept: Natalizumab is escalation (second-line) IV therapy for active MS.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 74-year-old patient with moderate Alzheimer disease is already receiving donepezil but shows progressive cognitive decline. The physician adds a drug that acts as an NMDA receptor antagonist to further improve symptoms. Which of the following drugs was most likely added?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is memantine, an NMDA-receptor antagonist added to a cholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil) in moderate-to-severe Alzheimer's disease.
questions.keyConcept: Memantine (NMDA antagonist) is added in moderate-severe Alzheimer's.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 74-year-old woman with Alzheimer's disease is started on therapy to improve her cognitive symptoms. After a few days, she develops abdominal cramps and frequent loose stools. Which of the following drugs is most likely responsible for this adverse effect?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is rivastigmine, a cholinesterase inhibitor whose cholinergic action commonly causes GI adverse effects such as abdominal cramps and diarrhea.
questions.keyConcept: Rivastigmine's cholinergic effect causes GI upset/diarrhea.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient presents with progressive muscle weakness, muscle wasting, fasciculations, and both upper and lower motor neuron signs, while sensory function remains intact. Which of the following drugs is used to slow disease progression in this condition?
questions.explanation: The picture of combined upper and lower motor neuron signs with intact sensation is ALS; the correct answer is riluzole, which slows progression by reducing glutamate excitotoxicity.
questions.keyConcept: ALS (UMN+LMN, sensation intact) is slowed by riluzole.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following antipsychotic medications is most associated with the potentially life-threatening side effect of agranulocytosis, requiring mandatory hematologic monitoring?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is clozapine, uniquely associated with agranulocytosis and therefore requiring mandatory blood-count monitoring; it is reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia.
questions.keyConcept: Clozapine causes agranulocytosis-mandatory blood-count monitoring.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following antipsychotic drugs is most commonly associated with agranulocytosis and therefore requires regular blood count monitoring?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is clozapine, the antipsychotic most associated with agranulocytosis, requiring regular blood counts during therapy.
questions.keyConcept: Clozapine requires regular monitoring for agranulocytosis.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient who has been receiving long-term antipsychotic therapy develops repetitive involuntary orofacial movements suggestive of tardive dyskinesia, an extrapyramidal side effect. Which of the following drugs is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is haloperidol; typical antipsychotics with strong D2 blockade most commonly cause tardive dyskinesia and other extrapyramidal effects.
questions.keyConcept: Haloperidol (typical antipsychotic) commonly causes tardive dyskinesia.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient experiencing severe nausea and vomiting after consuming alcohol while being treated for substance abuse is likely experiencing a reaction caused by which medication?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is disulfiram; by inhibiting aldehyde dehydrogenase it causes acetaldehyde accumulation, producing severe nausea and vomiting (the disulfiram-ethanol reaction) when alcohol is consumed.
questions.keyConcept: Disulfiram causes an aversive acetaldehyde reaction with alcohol.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A man who recently decided to quit smoking is prescribed a medication to reduce nicotine craving and decrease relapse rates during smoking cessation therapy. Which of the following drugs was most likely prescribed?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is varenicline, a partial nicotinic (alpha4beta2) acetylcholine-receptor agonist that reduces craving and relapse during smoking cessation.
questions.keyConcept: Varenicline (alpha4beta2 nicotinic partial agonist) aids smoking cessation.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: In unimmunized children infected with Poliovirus, which of the following is the most common clinical outcome?
options: Symptomatic febrile illness with muscle paralysis
questions.explanation: The correct answer is asymptomatic infection. The large majority (roughly 70 percent or more) of poliovirus infections in unimmunized children are asymptomatic; only a small minority develop paralytic or CNS disease.
questions.keyConcept: Most poliovirus infections are asymptomatic.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 4-year-old child presents with fever, vesicular lesions on the hands, feet, and inside the mouth, and mild malaise. Lumbar puncture shows CSF with normal glucose and normal opening pressure. Which of the following viruses is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Coxsackievirus. Fever with vesicular lesions on the hands, feet, and mouth and normal CSF indicates hand-foot-and-mouth disease, caused by Coxsackievirus (an enterovirus). HSV would instead cause temporal-lobe encephalitis.
questions.keyConcept: Coxsackievirus causes hand-foot-and-mouth disease.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 7-year-old boy presents with fever, headache, and neck stiffness. Lumbar puncture reveals elevated intracranial pressure, but cerebrospinal fluid protein and glucose levels are within normal limits. Question: Which of the following pathogens is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is Coxsackievirus. Raised pressure with normal CSF protein and glucose indicates viral (aseptic) meningitis; among the options the enterovirus Coxsackievirus fits, whereas bacterial/TB causes would lower glucose.
questions.keyConcept: Viral (aseptic) meningitis (Coxsackievirus) has normal CSF glucose.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Rabies virus reaches the central nervous system and spinal cord primarily through:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is neurons. Rabies virus reaches the CNS by retrograde axonal transport along peripheral neurons, not via blood, lymph, or CSF.
questions.keyConcept: Rabies spreads to the CNS via retrograde axonal (neuronal) transport.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Negri bodies are intracytoplasmic inclusions characteristic of which of the following infections?
